strengths: The paper is well-motivated: the empirical diagnostic in Section 3 clearly demonstrates that standard QE models (e.g., KIWI-XXL, XCOMET) exhibit high variance and reduced correlation when evaluated on translations with partial hallucinations and omissions.

The proposed framework (M2PO) is principled and coherent, successfully integrating alignment-based factuality penalties, dynamic weighting between static evaluators and policy probabilities, head-to-tail multi-pair construction, and stabilizing regularizers (LRank and LBC).
Experiments cover 10 language pairs across WMT benchmarks and show consistent improvements over competitive baselines, including ALMA-7B, standard DPO, and CPO.

Comprehensive ablation studies validate the necessity of each constituent loss component and module, and experiments across various preference algorithms (KTO, SimPO, ORPO, CPO) demonstrate good generality.
weaknesses: The evaluation relies almost exclusively on neural embedding-based metrics (COMET-22, XCOMET) and LLM-as-judge coverage scores; standard string-based metrics (such as SacreBLEU and chrF++) are absent, which is contrary to standard WMT evaluation reporting practices.

The faithfulness evaluation relies heavily on an LLM-as-judge prompt via Gemini-2.0-Flash that is uncalibrated against human annotations on the actual test set, and the prompt contains grammatical errors ('does the translation has hallucination...').

The candidate pool is partially constructed by querying GPT-4o-mini, making it difficult to fully disentangle the algorithmic preference gains from knowledge distillation of proprietary model outputs, despite the inclusion of an SFT baseline on the preference data.

strengths: Well-motivated empirical analysis: Section 3 provides a clear and insightful analysis on the HalOmi benchmark, quantitatively demonstrating that widely used QE metrics (XCOMET, KIWI-XXL) degrade notably when evaluating nuanced partial hallucinations and omissions compared to full errors.

Sound and cohesive framework: M2PO thoughtfully combines alignment-based hallucination penalties (WSPAlign) with QE, introduces an adaptive static-to-dynamic weighting curriculum, and efficiently utilizes candidate pools through head-to-tail multi-pairing with dynamic loss reweighting.

Extensive experimental evaluation: The proposed method is evaluated across 10 diverse language directions on WMT21-22 benchmarks, demonstrating consistent improvements over standard DPO, CPO, and SFT baselines, and performing competitively against proprietary models like GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4o.

Comprehensive validation and ablations: The authors demonstrate plug-and-play compatibility across diverse preference learning objectives (DPO, KTO, SimPO, ORPO, CPO) and provide thorough ablations confirming the individual contributions of the multi-pair strategy, dynamic scoring, and composite loss components.
weaknesses: Omission of standard lexical metrics: The empirical evaluation relies exclusively on neural metric variants (COMET-22, XCOMET, and an LLM-based Coverage score). Reporting standard surface-level metrics such as BLEU and chrF++ is standard in MT literature to verify that semantic and lexical precision are not degraded.

Reliance on LLM-as-a-judge for motivation and evaluation: The Coverage score relies on Gemini-2.0-Flash with a relatively simple zero-shot prompt. Using this metric both as the reference benchmark to expose QE flaws in Section 3 and as the primary metric for faithfulness in Section 5.3.3 introduces potential evaluator bias that is not deeply analyzed.

Hyperparameter complexity and sensitivity: The framework introduces multiple interacting hyperparameters (e.g., alignment bonus weight lambda_f, dynamic curriculum scheduler alpha_t, pair temperature tau_w, ListNet temperature tau_s, and loss weights lambda_pref, lambda_rank, lambda_bc). The paper lacks a sensitivity analysis examining how robust performance is to varying these choices.

Single model backbone: The experiments are conducted exclusively on the ALMA-7B-LoRA backbone. Demonstrating the approach on more modern open foundation models (e.g., Llama-3-8B or Qwen-2.5-7B) would significantly strengthen confidence in the generality of the method.

strengths: Well-motivated empirical analysis: Section 3 clearly demonstrates the blind spots of existing Quality Estimation (QE) models (XCOMET, KIWI-XXL) on partial translation hallucinations and omissions using the HalOmi benchmark.

Principled and cohesive framework design: Integrating word-level alignment (WSPAlign) with QE, curriculum-based dynamic scoring, multi-pair construction, and composite regularization (ListNet ranking and behavior cloning) provides an effective end-to-end recipe for MT preference tuning.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Evaluated across 10 translation directions (both English-to-X and X-to-English) on WMT21-22, demonstrating consistent improvements over standard SFT, DPO, and CPO baselines.

Broad applicability and thorough ablations: The authors validate that the framework acts as a general plug-in across diverse preference optimization algorithms (DPO, KTO, SimPO, ORPO, CPO) and perform clear ablations on all key loss components.
weaknesses: Absence of standard lexical metrics: The evaluation exclusively relies on neural metric models (COMET-22, XCOMET) and LLM-as-a-judge (Coverage Score). Standard surface metrics such as BLEU and ChrF++ should be included as essential sanity checks against length bias, repetition, or over-generation.

Lack of human evaluation: Given that the central premise of the work is correcting subtle hallucinations that automated metrics struggle with, the paper relies on an LLM-as-judge (Gemini 2.0 Flash) to evaluate faithfulness rather than conducting human evaluation or MQM error analysis.

Marginal sensitivity to pairing strategies: The experimental results in Table 5 show minimal differences across pairing strategies (e.g., Many-vs-Many vs. One-vs-Many differ by only ~0.1 XCOMET points), indicating that the gains from multi-pairing stem mostly from increased sample count rather than the proposed head-to-tail matching scheme.

Unreported computational complexity: Constructing pools of K=16 candidates, executing offline alignment/QE models, and computing dynamic forward passes over multiple pairs per instance incurs non-trivial computational overhead that is not quantified in terms of FLOPs, runtime, or memory requirements.
